name: Žleby Castle
region: Kutná Hora District, Central Bohemian Region — Žleby, between Čáslav and Třemošnice
architectural_style: Gothic-Renaissance château with Romantic neo-Gothic (Tudor-Gothic) remodel, mid-19th century — originally a Gothic castle of the 13th century, modified in Renaissance style in the 16th century; radically remodelled between the 1840s and 1880s by Karl Joseph, Prince Auersperg (1797–1886), who transformed the existing structure into a picturesque English Romantic Gothic composition with pointed turrets, stepped battlements, a neo-Gothic chapel, and richly decorated period interiors; the transformation drew directly on English Tudor and medieval-revival precedents fashionable among Central European aristocracy in the Romantic period; the surrounding English landscape park and artificial water features were designed as part of the same comprehensive 19th-century project; the interior includes a significant collection of period armour, weapons, and aristocratic furnishings preserved largely as the Auerspergs arranged them

opening_hours.seasonal_note: Open Tuesday–Sunday May through October; closed Monday and November–April. Last entry typically 16:00. Guided interior tours run at scheduled intervals — confirm current timetable at zamek-zleby.cz before visiting. The English landscape park has separate access hours and may be visited independently of the interior tour.

visit_duration: 1–1.5 hours (guided interior tour of state rooms, armor collection, neo-Gothic chapel); 30 minutes additional for the English landscape park
best_season: May to September — the château and park are at their best when the English landscape garden is in leaf; the autumn colour (October) is also worthwhile before closure. The neo-Gothic exterior is photogenic in all seasons.
accessibility: The guided interior tour involves stairs and period flooring. Not fully wheelchair accessible in the state rooms. The English landscape park is largely flat and accessible on gravel paths. Confirm specific requirements with the château before visiting.
tagline: Bohemia's most picturesque fairy-tale château — the Auersperg family's 19th-century Tudor-Gothic fantasy with turrets, armor halls, and an English landscape park
highlights: The Auersperg family's dramatic 19th-century Tudor-Gothic transformation — Karl Joseph, Prince Auersperg, spent the middle decades of the 19th century systematically remodelling a Renaissance château into an elaborate English Romantic Gothic composition: pointed turrets, stepped battlements, a neo-Gothic chapel, and interiors richly decorated with medieval-revival furnishings, creating one of the most visually striking 'fairy-tale' châteaux in Bohemia

Armor and weapons collection in period-furnished rooms — the château interior preserves a significant armory collection alongside the Auersperg family's furnishings, arranged largely as they were in the 19th century; the combination of authentic Gothic-revival interior design and real historical arms gives the rooms a character that reconstructed museum presentations rarely achieve

English landscape park with romantic water features — the 19th-century park surrounding the château was designed as an integral part of the Auersperg romantic vision, with mature specimen trees, artificial water, and carefully composed views of the château's turrets and battlements from the parkland; a classic Central European version of the English landscape aesthetic

Natural pairing with Kačina Castle — Žleby and Kačina Castle (approximately 20km northwest) are the two most rewarding Central Bohemia château visits outside Prague, routinely combined in a single day trip; the rational Empire-style neoclassicism of Kačina and the picturesque Romantic Gothic of Žleby represent opposite but complementary 19th-century architectural ambitions, and the GYG private tour covers both in the same day

Gothic chapel and the Auersperg family history — the neo-Gothic chapel built into the château complex is one of the best-preserved examples of 19th-century historicist ecclesiastical architecture in the Czech châteaux circuit; the Auersperg family — an important Austrian noble house with Bohemian landholdings — are represented throughout the interior through portraits, heraldry, and objects
description:
In the 1840s, Karl Joseph, Prince Auersperg, looked at the château his family held at Žleby in central Bohemia — a reasonably pleasant Renaissance building with Gothic foundations — and decided it needed to look entirely different. The result, completed over several decades, is one of the most consistently romantic and visually striking châteaux in the Czech Republic: a pointed-turret, stepped-battlements, neo-Gothic composition that quotes English medieval architecture in the manner fashionable among educated Central European aristocracy in the mid-19th century, set in a carefully composed English landscape park with artificial water and mature specimen trees.

The site at Žleby has a long history before the Auersperg transformation. A castle is first mentioned here in the 13th century, when the location on a gentle ridge above the Žlebský stream in central Bohemia was already recognised as a defensible position worth fortifying. The castle passed through the hands of several Bohemian noble families across the medieval and early modern centuries, accumulating the usual mixture of Gothic and Renaissance modifications, before arriving in the Auersperg family's possession in the 19th century. The Auerspergs were an Austrian noble house with extensive Bohemian landholdings and the cultural and financial resources to undertake a comprehensive architectural project — which is precisely what Karl Joseph did at Žleby.

The neo-Gothic movement in 19th-century Central European architecture was simultaneously a historicist exercise and a statement of Romantic sensibility. To build in the Gothic manner was to invoke the medieval past — the age of chivalry, of tournament and fealty, of a European aristocratic culture before the disruptions of revolution and industrial modernity. For Bohemian and Austrian nobles like the Auerspergs, it was also a way of asserting lineage and legitimacy through architectural reference rather than genealogical claim. Žleby's pointed turrets and stepped gables do not reproduce any specific medieval building; they synthesise medieval motifs into a picturesque composition that looks exactly as a 19th-century idea of a medieval castle should look, which is perhaps the purest expression of what the Romantic Gothic movement intended.

The interior is as carefully considered as the exterior. The state rooms combine authentic historical furnishings from several centuries of the château's occupation with the deliberate medieval-revival decorative programme that the Auersperg transformation introduced. The armory and weapons collection is the most distinctive element — a significant assembly of period armor and arms displayed in rooms whose architectural decoration gives them a specifically medieval atmosphere, reinforcing the collection's historical reach. The neo-Gothic chapel built into the complex is another outstanding element: a small but fully realised example of 19th-century historicist ecclesiastical architecture, with stained glass, decorated vault, and furnishings consistent with the overall Romantic programme.

The English landscape park surrounding the château was designed as an integral part of the Auersperg vision. The park's mature specimen trees, artificial water features, and carefully managed sightlines all function to present the château's exterior to maximum picturesque effect — the turrets are visible above the treeline from carefully chosen vantage points, the water reflects the battlements, and the parkland creates the impression of a medieval castle emerging from its natural setting rather than a 19th-century building site. The effect, particularly in the long light of late afternoon in spring or early autumn, is considerable.

Žleby is most naturally visited in combination with Kačina Castle, approximately 20km to the northwest. The two châteaux represent opposite but complementary strands of 19th-century aristocratic taste: Kačina's rational Empire-style neoclassicism — austere, symmetrical, confident — and Žleby's emotionally charged Gothic revivalism. Count Jan Rudolf Chotek and Prince Auersperg were peers in the Bohemian aristocracy of the same era, building in the same landscape within a generation of each other, and their architectural choices illuminate one of the central tensions in 19th-century European cultural life: the Enlightenment inheritance of classical reason versus the Romantic turn toward medieval history and natural emotion. The GYG private tour (t1369909) covers both châteaux from Prague in a single day.

[Kačina Castle](/castles/czech-republic/kacina-castle) — the finest Empire-style neoclassical château in the Czech Republic, built for Count Jan Rudolf Chotek between 1802 and 1822, with a 75,000-volume historic library and preserved theatre — is approximately 20km northwest of Žleby and is the standard day-trip pairing for visitors combining both sites.
history: 13th century: first castle at Žleby mentioned in records. 14th–15th century: Gothic castle developed and held by successive Bohemian noble families. 16th century: Renaissance modifications to the existing Gothic structure. 17th–early 19th century: château passes through further ownership; the Renaissance building maintained in modified form. 1840s–1880s: Karl Joseph, Prince Auersperg (1797–1886), undertakes comprehensive neo-Gothic (Tudor-Gothic/English Romantic) remodelling, transforming the château into its current picturesque form; English landscape park designed and planted in the same period. Late 19th–early 20th century: Auersperg family continue in possession; château furnished as a significant aristocratic seat. 20th century: confiscation after World War II and Czechoslovak nationalization decrees; château passes to state management. Present day: managed as a state museum château; guided tours May–October, Tuesday–Sunday.
how_to_visit:
**GYG private tour (~$1,191/group up to 3 people, t1369909, full day):** Private tour from Prague combining Kačina Castle and Žleby Castle in the same day; admission tickets to both châteaux, private transport, Czech lunch included. New activity — 0 reviews. Best option for covering both châteaux without individual car logistics.

**Independent visit:** Entry approximately 280 CZK (adults), open Tuesday–Sunday May–October. Žleby is approximately 75km east of Prague by road (D1 motorway then D35 and local roads); allow 1–1.5 hours by car. No direct public transport from Prague; combine with a car or taxi from Čáslav (the nearest town with rail connections). The château and park together take about 1.5–2 hours.

**Visiting in context:** Žleby and Kačina Castle make the natural day-trip pair from Prague for Central Bohemia château visits. Kutná Hora (UNESCO World Heritage silver-mining city, Cathedral of St Barbara, Sedlec Ossuary) is approximately 25km west of Žleby and can extend a day trip into a full programme.

faqs.question: What style is Žleby Castle and why does it look like an English medieval castle?
faqs.answer: Žleby's current appearance is the product of a mid-19th century Romantic neo-Gothic remodelling by Karl Joseph, Prince Auersperg. The style — often described as Tudor-Gothic or English Romantic Gothic — was fashionable among educated Central European aristocrats in the 19th century as a way of invoking the medieval past and expressing Romantic cultural values. The pointed turrets, stepped gables, battlements, and neo-Gothic chapel are all 19th-century additions to an earlier Renaissance building. The underlying structure is several centuries older than its exterior suggests. The same neo-Gothic movement produced comparable châteaux and castles across England, Germany, and the Czech lands in this period; Žleby is one of the most consistently realised Czech examples.

faqs.question: Can Žleby and Kačina be visited in the same day?
faqs.answer: Yes — Žleby and Kačina are approximately 20km apart and routinely combined in a single day trip from Prague or Kutná Hora. The two châteaux represent opposite 19th-century architectural ambitions: Kačina is the Empire-style neoclassical complement — rational, austere, symmetrical — to Žleby's emotionally charged Romantic Gothic. Together they cover a wide range of Bohemian aristocratic château culture from the early and mid-19th century. The GYG private tour (t1369909) runs exactly this combination from Prague with admission to both châteaux and a Czech lunch included.

faqs.question: What is in the armor collection at Žleby?
faqs.answer: The Žleby armory comprises a significant assembly of period armor and weapons — plate armor, swords, pole arms, and firearms from several centuries — displayed in the château's decorated state rooms. The collection was built up by the Auersperg family over generations and is presented in rooms whose neo-Gothic architectural decoration reinforces the medieval and early modern character of the arms on display. It is one of the more substantial private armory collections in the Czech château circuit, comparable in scope and atmosphere to the collections at châteaux with long aristocratic ownership histories elsewhere in Central Europe.
